theory.intro: A **network** (also called a **graph**) is a diagram of dots joined by lines. Each dot is a **vertex** (plural **vertices**) and each line joining two vertices is an **edge**. A network records only *what is joined to what*, so where a vertex sits on the page and how long or curved an edge is drawn carry no meaning at all — the same network can be drawn in many different ways. The **degree** of a vertex is the number of edge-ends meeting at it. An edge that leaves a vertex and returns to the same vertex is a **loop**, and because both of its ends are at that vertex it adds $2$ to the degree. Two vertices may be joined by more than one edge, and each of those **multiple edges** is counted separately. An edge that may only be travelled one way is **directed** and is drawn with an arrowhead, and an edge carrying a number such as a travel time is **weighted**.
facts: A **vertex** is a dot in the network; an **edge** is a line joining two vertices.
The **degree** of a vertex is the number of edge-ends meeting at it.
A **loop** joins a vertex to itself and contributes **$2$** to that vertex's degree.
**Multiple edges** between the same pair of vertices are allowed, and each one is counted separately.
Every edge has two ends, so the **sum of all the degrees is $2\times$ the number of edges** — and is therefore always even.
Two edges that cross on the page do **not** meet at a vertex unless a dot is actually drawn there.
A **directed** edge carries an arrowhead and may be travelled only in the direction of the arrow.
A **weighted** edge carries a number beside it giving a cost such as a time, a fare or a distance.
Only the connections matter, so moving the vertices around the page gives a **different drawing of the same network**.

$\deg A=1+1+2=4$, $\deg B=1+2=3$, $\deg C=2+1=3$, $\deg D=2$, $\deg E=2$.
$4+3+3+2+2$
$=14$
$14\div 2$
$=7$
Every edge, including a loop, has exactly two ends, so it adds $2$ to the total of the degrees.
**The degree sum is $14$, giving $7$ edges; the sum is a total of $2$s and so is always even.**

Sorting the second list gives $AB$, $AC$, $AE$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$ — exactly the same six pairs, and the degrees match as well ($A$ and $C$ have degree $3$; $B$, $D$ and $E$ have degree $2$).
How the vertices are arranged on the page carries no information.
**Ravi is incorrect — the same pairs are joined in both drawings, so they are one network drawn two different ways.**

A vertex exists only where a dot has been drawn, and no dot is drawn at the crossing.
Because the roads pass over one another, a driver on $AD$ cannot change to $BE$ there, so no edge-ends meet and the crossing has no degree at all.
The vertices are $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, and the edges are $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$, $EF$, $FA$, $AD$, $BE$.
**Jo has counted a crossing as a vertex; the network really has $6$ vertices and $8$ edges.**
